item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK -- Days before the start of what could be Major League Baseball's last postseason for a while, Carlos Rodon was prepared for a long lockout if owners keep their salary cap proposal on the bargaining table.
"We won't play. I'm going to be frank with you," the New York Yankees pitcher said. "I'm not worried about it. They should be worried about it. There's a lot of money on us playing baseball. That's why they pay us a lot."
Baseball's five-year labor contract expires Dec. 1 and management is expected to impose a lockout that would stop trades and free-agent signings, then potentially threaten the start of spring training workouts on Feb. 9 and opening day on March 24.
When management last proposed a cap, it sparked a 7 1/2-month strike in 1994 and '95 that led to the first cancellation of the World Series in 90 years. MLB says a cap is needed to alleviate economic disparity, highlighting that no low-revenue team has won the title since the 2015 Kansas City Royals.
"The salary cap and floor proposal levels the playing field, allowing us greater flexibility to address longstanding player priorities while sharing baseball revenue with the players 50/50," MLB spokesman Glen Caplin said.
Owners would also gain more financial certainty with a cap, which likely would spark an increase in franchise values.
Players point out teams with low payrolls, Milwaukee and Tampa Bay, had the best regular-season records in their leagues this season.
"Despite MLB claiming they need a salary cap because small-market teams supposedly have no hope, we see Milwaukee with the best record in baseball for the second straight year and Tampa with the best record in the AL," union head Bruce Meyer said. "Milwaukee, of course, is 30th out of 30 in our market-size rankings."
While this would be MLB's 10th work stoppage, the sport hasn't lost any regular-season games since the 1994-95 strike. Baseball players say they will never accept a cap similar to those that have been in the NFL since 1994, the NBA since 1984-85 and the NHL since 2005-06. Nine of the 10 biggest sports contracts by total value in North America belong to MLB players.
"For me the biggest thing is doing right for the generations forward because the generations before me, for the decades before, they've fought for our rights today," Baltimore first baseman Pete Alonso said. "That's a sacrifice that not just myself but other men around the league are willing to fight for and put up with."
MLB's proposal would cap team spending next year at $245.3 million, using figures for luxury tax payrolls that include an estimated $23 million for benefits and the pre-arbitration bonus pool. It also would establish a payroll floor of $171.2 million for 2027 but teams could drop as low as $154.1 million and make up the difference over the following two years. The New York Mets' opening day payroll in 2026 was more than $352 million.
Contracts would be limited by service time: $500 million and 12 years for those yet to make major league debuts down to $265 million and six years for free-agent-eligible players. It would outlaw megadeals like outfielder Juan Soto's record 15-year, $765 million contract with the Mets.
While MLB proposed to split revenues 50-50, the union says that would lead to a massive decrease in money to players because of the way revenues and expenses are defined and the player portion is calculated. In addition, an escrow provision to set salaries aside in case the players' defined revenue share is above 50% means money in guaranteed contracts could be forfeited.
MLB as part of a cap system would agree to drop service time for free agent eligibility for some players from six years of service to five and to eliminate qualifying offers, but the union maintains that would shift money among players under a cap rather than increase spending.
Alonso would lose $165,775 next year for each regular-season day missed and Rodon would forfeit $144,385.
Los Angeles Dodgers star Shohei Ohtani would give up $374,331 daily and Soto $227,273.
At the other end of the salary scale, players making MLB's proposed $900,000 minimum would lose $4,813 daily. Among the 1,366 players on rosters as of Monday, 549 (40%) started 2026 with less than one year of service time and 893 (65%) had less than three years. Players aren't eligible for salary arbitration until they've completed three seasons, with some exceptions.
Some players are protected financially because of signing bonuses that will continue to be paid during a work stoppage: Toronto first baseman Vladimir Guerrero Jr. is due $14 million on June 30 as part of his $325 million contract, though he would give up $74,866 daily in salary.
Tony Clark, the former All-Star first baseman who had headed the union since 2013, was forced out in February and replaced by Meyer, his deputy and chief negotiator in 2021-22.
Baltimore pitcher Chris Bassitt, a member of the union's eight-man executive subcommittee, said there had been a transformation this year in communications within the players' association. The subcommittee and the 30 team player representatives form the executive council that makes union decisions.
"Our last CBA from a player's side was not internally handled great. I think the structure was very archaic, so to speak, like an old-school approach," he said. "We have made it our mission to kind of get all 30 clubs -- 30 reps that genuinely care. And then not just 30 reps that genuinely care, but 30 reps that are making sure all their players are very informed."
When players and MLB agreed to a deal on March 10, 2022, that ended the lockout, the executive subcommittee voted 8-0 against accepting it, but the team player representatives favored the agreement by 26-4.
The vast majority of the 1,200 players on 40-man rosters when the lockout starts will not have salary arbitration or free agency rights and will have 2027 salaries under $1 million.
"Their voices matter, what they're feeling, what they're thinking," Bassitt said. "When I came in the league it was -- I'm going to say it plainly -- but it was like: 'Rookie shut up and sit in the corner and the veterans are going to take care of this.' I don't think that's a possible avenue to go down anymore. I think the league's too young, first and foremost. Second, I think the only way to have veteran guys that are informed and understand the process is to start the education process from day one."

item.title: [marca usa] Las dos estrellas de los Mets que cargan con la mayor responsabilidad por una temporada desastrosa
item.dc:creator: Jose Rodriguez
item.description: - MLB. La última apertura de Justin Verlander marca el final de una carrera brillante - MLB. Las lesiones, una construcción deficiente del roste
item.content:encoded:
- MLB. La última apertura de Justin Verlander marca el final de una carrera brillante
- MLB. Vladimir Guerrero Jr. consigue uno de los sencillos productores más extraños del béisbol
Los New York Mets no solo se quedaron fuera de los playoffs en 2026. Se desplomaron. Con un récord de 74-88, un último lugar en la División Este de la Liga Nacional y una de las nóminas más altas de las Grandes Ligas, la temporada terminó siendo un completo fracaso. Las lesiones, una construcción deficiente del roster y el bajo rendimiento general fueron factores importantes, por lo que no toda la responsabilidad puede recaer sobre dos jugadores.
Sin embargo, la rendición de cuentas debe comenzar con quienes estaban llamados a liderar al equipo. Francisco Lindor debía ser el corazón de la franquicia, mientras que Jorge Polanco llegó como un bateador veterano confiable. En cambio, ambos terminaron simbolizando una campaña en la que el talento más caro y probado estuvo muy lejos de responder a las expectativas de Nueva York.
Francisco Lindor nunca jugó como la estrella franquicia que esperaban los Mets
Lindor merece cierto contexto. Se sometió a una cirugía en el codo durante el invierno, sufrió una fractura del hueso ganchoso de la mano durante los entrenamientos y posteriormente estuvo cerca de dos meses fuera por una distensión en la pantorrilla. Con tantas interrupciones, encontrar ritmo fue prácticamente imposible.
Aun así, los Mets necesitaban una superestrella, no solo un jugador disponible en la alineación, y pocas veces la tuvieron. Lindor bateó para .225, con un porcentaje de embasado (.309), slugging (.423) y un OPS de .732, el más bajo de toda su carrera. Conectó 21 cuadrangulares, pero apenas produjo 49 carreras impulsadas en 105 juegos.
Su retroceso no se limitó al bate. Cometió 11 errores, la mayor cifra de su carrera, y terminó por debajo del promedio en la métrica Outs Above Average de Statcast. Un análisis sobre el rendimiento de los Mets de un año a otro mostró que su aporte cayó de 6.1 WAR en 2025 a una proyección de apenas 1.9 WAR en 2026, la mayor disminución entre las principales figuras que regresaron al equipo.
Nada de esto convierte a Lindor en un mal jugador, y las lesiones fueron un factor real. Pero cuando una franquicia está construida alrededor de un campocorto superestrella, perder más de cuatro victorias de valor esperado puede hundir una temporada. Los Mets confiaban en tener una ventaja clara en el shortstop y terminaron sin estabilidad ni excelencia en ambos lados del terreno.
Jorge Polanco fue el mayor problema de la alineación
Si Lindor representó la mayor decepción por las expectativas que existían sobre él, Jorge Polanco fue quien más perjudicó al equipo por sus resultados. Los Mets le otorgaron un contrato de dos años y 40 millones de dólares después de que conectara 26 cuadrangulares y registrara un OPS de .821 con Seattle en 2025, esperando que aportara profundidad y poder al lineup.
Lo que recibieron fue una de las peores temporadas ofensivas de todo el béisbol: promedio de .148, porcentaje de embasado de .201, slugging de .230, apenas dos jonrones y seis carreras impulsadas en 145 apariciones al plato. Además, fue utilizado casi exclusivamente como bateador designado, por lo que tampoco pudo compensar su bajo rendimiento con el guante. Tanto FanGraphs como Baseball Reference lo evaluaron con -1.4 WAR pese a disputar un número limitado de juegos.
Las lesiones en la muñeca, el tendón de Aquiles y el tobillo lo acompañaron durante toda la campaña, hasta que una cirugía en el tobillo puso fin a su temporada en agosto. Eso explica parte del desplome, pero no su impacto. Un bateador designado existe para producir ofensivamente, y Polanco ocupó un lugar en la alineación sin aportar poder, promedio ni capacidad para embasarse.
La oficina principal también merece críticas por construir un roster frágil, y las lesiones nunca dejaron de aparecer. Aun así, Lindor y Polanco sobresalen porque su producción estuvo muy por debajo del rol que debían desempeñar. La falta de liderazgo de Lindor le quitó a los Mets la base de su proyecto, mientras que el bate de Polanco convirtió una de las principales inversiones del invierno en un peso muerto. Ellos no fueron los únicos responsables de las 88 derrotas, pero sí representan mejor que nadie por qué un equipo diseñado para competir terminó hundido en el último lugar.

item.title: [jaysjournal.com] Blue Jays 2026 report card: Grading an offence that ranked among MLB’s worst
item.dc:creator: Ben Wrixon
item.description: The Toronto Blue Jays entered 2026 expecting their offence to help carry them to another postseason run. Instead, a lineup that had been central to the club’s World Series appearance a year earlier became one of its biggest weaknesses. Established stars endured dramatic downturns, useful role players were asked to carry larger workloads and injuries forced Toronto to lean on several inexperienced hitters. item.content:encoded:
The Toronto Blue Jays entered 2026 expecting their offence to help carry them to another postseason run. Instead, a lineup that had been central to the club’s World Series appearance a year earlier became one of its biggest weaknesses. Established stars endured dramatic downturns, useful role players were asked to carry larger workloads and injuries forced Toronto to lean on several inexperienced hitters.
Anyone who watched the Blue Jays in 2026 knows they were not a good offensive team. They scored the fewest runs in all of baseball (648), hit the fewest home runs (152), and ranked second-worst in team OPS (.691) ahead of only the Los Angeles Angels.
There were still a few encouraging performances. But for every one of those successes they Blue Jays had another two or three hitters who fell short of expectations. The grades below weigh each hitter’s production against his role, opportunity and expectations entering the season.
Grading every Blue Jays hitter from the 2026 season
Alejandro Kirk
- HR: 10
- RBI: 43
- AVG: .278
- OPS: .767
- wRC+: 114
Kirk didn’t look like himself to start the year, then missed several months with a thumb injury. He recaptured his All-Star form when he finally returned, however, and led the Blue Jays offensively for much of the second half.
Grade: B+
Andrés Giménez
- HR: 9
- RBI: 59
- AVG: .244
- OPS: .649
- wRC+: 81
Giménez is what he is at this point: a below-average hitter with a knack for coming through in the clutch. He still managed to accrue 2.8 fWAR on the strength of his stellar glovework at shortstop and contributions on the basepaths.
Grade: B-
Brandon Valenzuela
- HR: 9
- RBI: 24
- AVG: .226
- OPS: .688
- wRC+: 96
Valenzuela filled in admirably for Kirk while he was on the injured list during the first half of the season. He flashed legitimate power upside at the plate before going ice-cold after the All-Star break, exposing the current limitations of his offensive profile.
Grade: C
Brett Bateman
- HR: 2
- RBI: 11
- AVG: .329
- OPS: .826
- wRC+: 138
Bateman exceeded all expectations after being acquired for Kevin Gausman at the trade deadline. He injected some life into the lineup immediately upon arrival and has likely cemented himself as a marquee piece of the 2027 squad.
Grade: A+
Charles McAdoo
- HR: 3
- RBI: 14
- AVG: .258
- OPS: .694
- wRC+: 93
McAdoo largely held his own at the plate with the Blue Jays in 2026. His approach needs work, but his combination of power and speed is exciting. He should keep improving with additional reps against MLB pitching.
Grade: C+
Davis Schneider
- HR: 5
- RBI: 16
- AVG: .145
- OPS: .624
- wRC+: 84
Schneider was one of several surprise contributors who propelled the Blue Jays to the World Series in 2025. His production fell off a cliff this year, which led to multiple demotions to Triple-A Buffalo. He might be out of runway.
Grade: F
Ernie Clement
- HR: 9
- RBI: 48
- AVG: .259
- OPS: .649
- wRC+: 80
It was a tale of two seasons for Clement. He rode a strong first half to his first career All-Star appearance, then devolved into one of baseball’s worst hitters from August onward. He ended the year with the worst offensive numbers of his career.
Grade: C-
George Springer
- HR: 15
- RBI: 54
- AVG: .249
- OPS: .726
- wRC+: 105
Springer redeemed what was likely his final season with the Blue Jays with a strong second half. While he didn’t come anywhere near his 2025 numbers, he still put together a solid season. His contract was worth every penny.
Grade: B-
Jésus Sánchez
- HR: 8
- RBI: 35
- AVG: .254
- OPS: .713
- wRC+: 99
He makes the list because he was on the team for most of the year before being designated for assignment in September. He failed to turn his power potential into actual production, and the less that can be said about his defence, the better.
Grade: D
Josh Smith
- HR: 6
- RBI: 15
- AVG: .203
- OPS: .611
- wRC+: 75
Smith was a pleasant surprise down the stretch after coming over in the Adam Macko trade, hitting five of his six home runs after coming to Toronto. He should have an opportunity to compete for a bench spot on the 2027 squad.
Grade: B-
Kazuma Okamoto
- HR: 33
- RBI: 92
- AVG: .232
- OPS: .762
- wRC+: 113
The general consensus on Okamoto coming over from Japan was that he would hit for a high average with some power. He ended up being more of a three true outcome guy who led the team in home runs, RBI, and strikeouts by a wide margin.
Grade: B+
Myles Straw
- HR: 3
- RBI: 26
- AVG: .241
- OPS: .646
- wRC+: 83
Straw wound up getting far more plate appearances than anyone expected he would coming into the year. Unsurprisingly, he didn’t do much with those opportunities. His value is in his speed, excellent defensive play, and clubhouse presence.
Grade: C+
Nathan Lukes:
- HR: 10
- RBI: 41
- AVG: .277
- OPS: .725
- wRC+: 102
Lukes got off to an extremely rough start at the plate while managing a bout of vertigo, but eventually settled back into his usual form. He’s a league-average hitter who grinds out at-bats—a quintessentially glue guy in a deeper lineup.
Grade: B
Sean Keys
- HR: 2
- RBI: 9
- AVG: .197
- OPS: .570
- wRC+: 57
Assigning Keys a letter grade almost feels unfair given how little he played. Still, he flashed some power potential in his limited opportunities, albeit while appearing generally overmatched by major league pitching. He’s very much a work in progress.
Grade: C
Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
- HR: 9
- RBI: 57
- AVG: .260
- OPS: .688
- wRC+: 95
This might be the most disappointing season by a hitter in the 50-year history of the franchise. Coming off a historic postseason, Guerrero authored one of the most pathetic performances by a superstar in recent memory. That ridiculous quote didn’t help, either.
Grade: F

item.content:encoded:
Vladimir Guerrero Jr. consiguió un sencillo productor tan extraño que fue necesaria una repetición en cámara lenta para entenderlo.
Con récord de 0-2 ante el relevista de los Reds Luis Mey, Guerrero golpeó un sinker hacia el centro mientras su bate se rompía.
El barril roto cayó frente al plato y golpeó la pelota por segunda vez, desviándose hacia el lado derecho del infield y permitiendo que entrara una carrera.
Según las reglas de MLB, la jugada continúa cuando una pelota bateada golpea un fragmento del bate roto en territorio bueno. El insólito sencillo ayudó a iniciar una séptima entrada de cuatro carreras para Toronto en su dramática victoria por 6-5.
Pareció un caos absoluto, pero en el box score fue simplemente otra carrera impulsada para Guerrero.

item.dc:creator: Angel Nakamura
item.description: Vladimir Guerrero Jr. has produced plenty of memorable hits during his career, but few have looked quite like the one he delivered Friday night against the Reds. The Blue Jays first baseman helped ignite a decisive seventh-inning rally in Toronto's 6-5 victory at Rogers Centre with an RBI single that required a bit of baseball luck, and an unexpected assist from his broken bat. item.content:encoded:
Vladimir Guerrero Jr. has produced plenty of memorable hits during his career, but few have looked quite like the one he delivered Friday night against the Reds.
The Blue Jays first baseman helped ignite a decisive seventh-inning rally in Toronto's 6-5 victory at Rogers Centre with an RBI single that required a bit of baseball luck, and an unexpected assist from his broken bat.
Facing Cincinnati reliever Luis Mey with an 0-2 count, Guerrero swung at a sinker and chopped a ground ball toward the middle of the infield. As he made contact, the bat shattered.
Slow-motion replay revealed a remarkable sequence. After the ball initially came off Guerrero's bat, the severed barrel landed several feet in front of home plate and made contact with the baseball a second time. The unexpected deflection altered the ball's path, sending it toward the right side of the infield.

item.content:encoded:
It hasn't been the 2026 campaign Vladimir Guerrero Jr. or the Toronto Blue Jays have hoped for by any stretch this season.
Toronto reached the World Series less than a year ago and came just inches away from winning it, but the Blue Jays will miss the postseason this year.
On Saturday, they'll play their second-to-last game of the regular season as they come off a 6-5 win over the Cincinnati Reds on Friday night in their series opener.
Ahead of Game 2 of the weekend set, Blue Jays manager John Schneider announced a notable lineup change involving Guerrero Jr.
Blue Jays Announce Guerrero Jr. Decision
After starting at first base on Friday and recording one hit and an RBI, Guerrero Jr. is back in the lineup again but will transition to designated hitter while batting third in the order, behind Brett Bateman, who returns to the lineup, and Nathan Lukes.
Here's the full Blue Jays lineup:
Via Underdog MLB: "Blue Jays 9/26 B. Bateman CF N. Lukes RF V. Guerrero Jr. DH A. Kirk C K. Okamoto 3B S. Keys 1B J. Smith LF A. Giménez SS E. Clement 2B T. Yesavage SP."
Guerrero Jr.'s 2026 Season
While the Blue Jays star was once again named an All-Star for the sixth straight year, he simply lacked power this season.
He's appeared in 142 games for Toronto in 2026 and, across 533 at-bats, he's hitting .263 with 71 runs, 140 hits, nine home runs, and 56 RBIs while slugging just .360 with a .695 OPS.
Guerrero Jr. made it very clear over the last few days that he plans on living up to the massive 14-year, $500 million contract he signed in 2025 after stirring up some controversy with comments earlier in the week.
He has since apologized for saying the Blue Jays paid him for what he's already accomplished, not what he's going to do in the future, and has retracted those statements.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Toronto Blue Jays Announce Vladimir Guerrero Jr. Decision During Reds Series appeared first on HEAVY.

item.content:encoded:
Throughout the season, the California Post power-ranked MLB’s 30 teams and checked in on intriguing awards races. Records as of Saturday morning:
1) Brewers (101-59): A+
It was another perfect regular season for the Brewers, who won 100 games for the first time in franchise history to clinch the best record in the majors. Of course, their repeated failures in recent postseasons mean the real test is still to come in October. They have one superstar in Jacob Misiorowski but will need others to emerge in this year’s playoffs.
2) Dodgers (98-62): A
It was a familiar story for the Dodgers this year. A hot start. A second-half slump. Plenty of injuries along the way. Yet, another division crown that sets them up for another deep October run. That formula has worked the past two years for the two-time defending champions. Their real grade this season will depend on whether they can complete a World Series three-peat.
3) Rays (97-63): A+
After two years of missing the playoffs, the Rays had a very Rays-esque season. Uncovered gems on the mound. A relentlessly consistent lineup at the plate. And, as a result, the AL’s best record — and their best chance to get back to the World Series since 2020.
4) Braves (93-67): A
The Braves are back in the playoffs and back atop the NL East, rebounding as hoped from a disappointing 86-loss campaign last season that snapped a six-year postseason streak.
5) Yankees (93-68): B+
This grade might’ve been higher, if not for the uncertainty shrouding the Bronx Bombers as they enter the postseason. They managed to survive one extended Aaron Judge absence this regular season. Trying to do so again in October would be a tall task.
6) Padres (89-71): A-
In the weeks leading up to the trade deadline, the Padres seemed bound to be sellers. But then their offense — especially Fernando Tatis Jr. — came back to life. They bolstered their rotation by being buyers at the trade deadline instead. And now they are back in the playoffs as a potential dark horse, thanks to their 16-5 record in September.
7) Cubs (88-73): B+
The Cubs are back in the playoffs for a second straight year. They have the presumptive National League MVP in Pete Crow-Armstrong. And they managed to overcome a wave of pitching injuries. Now, they will try to mount a deeper October run after being knocked out in Game 5 of the NLDS last year.
8) Red Sox (87-74): B+
A strange regular season in Boston has reached a satisfactory ending, with the Red Sox — led by interim-now-turned-permanent manager Chad Tracy — getting a shot to avenge last year’s postseason elimination to the Yankees in next week’s wild-card series.
9) Phillies (87-73): Incomplete
Check back with us on Sunday night for this final grade. Because after seemingly salvaging their nightmarish start to the season under interim manager Don Mattingly, the Phillies are flirting with what would be a monumental September collapse, having yet to secure their place in the playoffs amid a 2-5 slump this week.
10) Diamondbacks (86-74): B-
We are only tentatively grading the Dbacks for now, thanks to their slim (but very much possible) chances of sneaking into the playoffs. If they don’t, it will be another conflicting season for the Dbacks, who have won 80-plus games in four straight seasons but still have just their surprise 2023 World Series run to show for it.
11) Guardians (84-76): A
The Guardians did what they do this season. Prevent runs. Score just enough. Fly under the radar for most of the year. Then round into form late to (most likely) win another AL Central title.
12) White Sox (83-77): A
This could still become an A+ if the White Sox wind up winning the AL Central. But even if not, the South Siders have been the most pleasant surprise in the majors this season, going from three straight 100-loss seasons to an upstart playoff berth with their young and promising roster.
13/14) Astros/Rangers (79-81): Incomplete
To be clear, neither of these teams has had a good 2026. And yet, they both enter the final days of the season with a chance to win the AL West — even though they can finish no better than .500. It will be the first time in MLB history a team will make the playoffs without a winning record. What a year in the AL West.
15) Pirates (81-79): C+
Good news: The Pirates avoided a losing record for the first time since 2018. Bad news: It wasn’t enough to keep them in playoff contention despite a surprisingly productive year from their offense.
16) Marlins (79-81): C+
The Marlins flirted with playoff contention for a while before ultimately fading down the stretch. They could be poised to take another step next year. Then again, they’ve looked that way before (remember that surprise playoff appearance in 2023?) and been unable to keep progressing.
17) Orioles (79-82): D
The Orioles’ signing of Pete Alonso worked out. But little else did in Baltimore this year. The once-budding contender has now missed the playoffs in two straight years after being swept in back-to-back postseasons the two years before that.
18) Blue Jays (78-82): D
As if the Blue Jays’ post-pennant campaign wasn’t bad enough, Vladimir Guerrero Jr. provided one more low point with his comments about his $500 million contract this week. There is hope for next season. But this year stung.
19) Cardinals (77-83): B
Given nonexistent preseason expectations, the rebuilding Cardinals mostly accomplished what they wanted to this year. They have young talent in Jordan Walker and JJ Wetherholt. They have rebuilt what is now a highly ranked farm system. And they look like a team capable of making a jump in 2027 and beyond.
20) Nationals (76-84): C
The Nats were never serious playoff contenders (their MLB-record 42 blown saves made sure of that). But they have identified a core of young talent to build around. Whether they will spend to add the necessary pieces around them, however, remains to be seen.
21) Mets (73-87): D-
The Mets can only hope this train wreck of a year serves as some sort of cleanse as they look to retool their roster this winter. The only thing that saved this from being an F was their second-half performance under another interim-now-turned-permanent manager in Andy Green.
22) Twins (76-84): C
For some reason, the Twins were intent on being playoff contenders this year. For a while, they hung around in a bad AL wild-card race. But in the end, they’ve wound up back where they started: With an OK, but not-at-all contending, roster that leaves them stuck in MLB’s no-man’s land.
23) Tigers (75-85): D
How much will the Tigers rue their decision to not maximize Tarik Skubal’s trade value by dealing him last winter? It could depend, first and foremost, on River Ryan’s development in their rotation. At the least, he offered signs of promise with a scoreless three-inning debut with the team this week.
24) Reds (74-86): D
Whatever momentum the Reds thought they were building after last year’s postseason berth vanished this summer, despite Elly De La Cruz cementing himself as one of the best players in baseball. The next time their owner asks why they aren’t the Brewers, someone should hold up a mirror.
25) Mariners (74-86): F
At the beginning of the year, only the Dodgers had a higher probability of making the playoffs (according to FanGraphs’ computer models) than the Mariners’ 80.9% mark. Instead, they suffered what might be the most disappointing season in their long-tortured history. They could be good again next year. But this season was a reminder that’s anything but a guarantee.
26) Royals (68-92): D
Another disastrous Royals season leaves them facing an existential crisis, trying to figure out how to return to competitiveness before they waste the prime of Bobby Witt Jr.’s career.
27) Giants (65-95): F
The Giants thought they could be contenders this year. Instead, they now find themselves at a crossroads. They have little choice but to run it back with their thus-far disappointing core of Willy Adames, Matt Chapman and Rafael Devers (plus Logan Webb). But this year, they looked a long way off from even being competitive.
28) Athletics (64-96): D-
There was some thought before the year that the Athletics’ young roster could be feisty. Now, the only question is how much longer they have to waste away in their minor-league ballpark purgatory.
29) Angels (62-98): C
This grade has little to do with the Angels’ on-field product, as they flirt with what would be the first 100-loss season in franchise history, and everything to do with the changes they’ve made behind the scenes. New owner. New front office. And for the first time in a while, new reason for long-term hope.
30) Rockies (57-103): D
The best thing we can say about the Rockies: They proved slightly tougher to beat during this 100-loss season, as opposed to each of the three previous ones they have suffered the last three years. Progress!
Awards Predictions
NL MVP: Pete Crow-Armstrong, Cubs
AL MVP: Yordan Alvarez, Astros
NL Cy Young: Jacob Misiorowski, Brewers
AL Cy Young: Cam Schlittler, Yankees
NL Rookie of the Year: Sal Stewart, Reds
AL Rookie of the Year: Kevin McGonigle, Tigers
NL Reliever of the Year: Mason Miller, Padres
AL Reliever of the Year: Louis Varland, Blue Jays

item.content:encoded:
이런 더블 히트(두 번 맞추는 안타)를 본 적이 있으십니까?
제대로 배트 중심에 맞았다고 말할 수 있는 순간이었습니다.
토론토 블루제이스의 1루수 블라디미르 게레로 주니어는 25일(미국 현지시간) 로저스 센터에서 열린 신시내티 레즈와의 경기에서 6-5 승리를 거둔 7회초에 기술적으로 타점 적시타를 만들어냈지만, 그 과정은 꽤나 특이했습니다.
신시내티의 불펜 투수 루이스 메이의 0-2 카운트 싱커를 상대로, 게레로는 가운데 방향으로 땅볼을 쳐냈고 그 과정에서 배트가 두 토막으로 부러졌습니다. 그러자 순수한 야구의 마법이 펼쳐졌습니다.
슬로모션 리플레이는 정확히 무슨 일이 일어났는지 보여주었습니다. 게레로의 부러진 배트 동체 조각이 홈플레이트 전방 수 피트 앞에서 야구공과 다시 부딪히며 공의 진로를 내야 오른쪽 방향으로 꺾어놓았습니다. 공은 레즈 수비진의 빈틈을 굴러 우익수 앞 안타가 되었고, 2루에 있던 안드레스 히메네스를 홈으로 불러들였습니다.
토론토에 리드를 안기고 결국 승리로 이어진 결정적인 7회 4득점 빅이닝의 첫 득점을 만들어낸 게레로의 이 안타는 선수가 공을 두 번 치는 일이 발생한 최초의 안타가 결코 아니었습니다. 사실, 하루에만 두 번 나온 사례를 포함하여 이번 시즌에만 적어도 여섯 번째로 발생한 일입니다.
게레로가 머릿속으로 그리던 완벽한 정타는 분명 아니었지만, 금요일에 나온 이 더블 히트는 진정 기발한 방식으로 "수비가 없는 곳으로 타구를 보내는" 결과를 만들어냈습니다.

item.title: [bolavip.com] Blue Jays’ Vladimir Guerrero Jr. regrets past comments, discusses contract extension
item.dc:creator: Santiago Tovar
item.description: Fresh off a run as the AL pennant runners-up last season, the Toronto Blue Jays have officially been eliminated from 2026 postseason contention. Toronto has turned its focus toward next year—and to expecting a return to form from star slugger Vladimir Guerrero Jr., who signed a massive contract extension with the club. However, recent comments from Guerrero Jr. sparked a firestorm among the fan base over the week. On Friday, the first baseman spoke to the media alongside his Hall of Fame father
item.content:encoded:
Fresh off a run as the AL pennant runners-up last season, the Toronto Blue Jays have officially been eliminated from 2026 postseason contention. Toronto has turned its focus toward next year—and to expecting a return to form from star slugger Vladimir Guerrero Jr., who signed a massive contract extension with the club.
However, recent comments from Guerrero Jr. sparked a firestorm among the fan base over the week. On Friday, the first baseman spoke to the media alongside his Hall of Fame father to address the controversy and express regret over his statement. “I feel like the comments I made the other day didn’t accurately reflect what I really wanted to say. Everyone deserves an apology from me,” Guerrero Jr. told reporters.
Guerrero ignited a wave of backlash across social media after an interview posted by content creator Masterflip, during which the slugger remarked that the Blue Jays “didn’t pay me to hit 40 [home runs] every year.”
While other MLB contenders scratch and claw for a postseason berth—such as the Philadelphia Phillies, who missed an opportunity to lock up their spot heading into October—the Blue Jays find themselves navigating internal turbulence surrounding the face of their franchise.
Vladimir Guerrero Jr. #27 of the Toronto Blue Jays.
Vladdy’s struggles this season
Following a dominant 2025 campaign, Guerrero Jr. has endured a surprisingly down year. His lingering struggles at the plate are reflected in his numbers: just nine home runs and 56 RBIs through 142 games.
Guerrero has been hampered by various nagging injuries throughout the year, missing around 17 games. Playing through constant physical discomfort has prevented him from finding a rhythm or establishing consistent timing in the batter’s box.
MLB legend weighs in on Guerrero Jr.’s comments
Addressing the noise surrounding the Toronto star, MLB legend Pedro Martinez stepped up to defend Guerrero Jr.’s intent. “He was misinterpreted. What he meant is that contract came from what he’s already done and what he can still do,” Martinez said to El Emergente’s Marcos Grunfeld. “That’s a young man talking—he just didn’t explain himself the right way.”
Despite the current turmoil, Vladdy still has plenty of time to prove that his long-term contract extension was well-earned. If he can turn things around next spring, he remains positioned to re-establish himself as one of the premier hitters in Major League Baseball.
Key takeaways
- Vladimir Guerrero Jr. apologized for recent comments that sparked backlash among fans.
- MLB legend Pedro Martinez defended the slugger, stating his comments were misinterpreted.
- The Toronto Blue Jays have been officially eliminated from 2026 postseason contention.

item.content:encoded:
Las Grandes Ligas de Béisbol (MLB, por sus siglas en inglés) revelaron las 20 camisetas de peloteros más vendidas de la temporada 2026.
En la lista figura un solo pelotero venezolano: Ronald Acuña Jr., de los Bravos de Atlanta, quien ocupa la cuarta posición. En 2025, Acuña Jr. también figuró en este listado, pero en el puesto 11.
La publicación, difundida por la MLB en su cuenta de Instagram, reveló que el japonés Shohei Ohtani, de los Dodgers de Los Ángeles, encabeza la lista de las camisetas más vendidas.
En cuanto a los equipos, los Dodgers de Los Ángeles son los que cuentan con más jugadores en la lista, con cuatro: Ohtani, Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts y Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
¿Quiénes son los 20 peloteros con las camisetas más vendidas en 2026?
De acuerdo con la lista difundida por la MLB, estas son las 20 camisetas más vendidas de la temporada 2026:
- Shohei Ohtani, Dodgers de Los Ángeles.
- Aaron Judge, Yankees de Nueva York.
- Pete Crow-Armstrong, Cachorros de Chicago.
- Ronald Acuña Jr., Bravos de Atlanta.
- Fernando Tatis Jr., Padres de San Diego.
- Freddie Freeman, Dodgers de Los Ángeles.
- Bryce Harper, Filis de Filadelfia.
- Mookie Betts, Dodgers de Los Ángeles.
- Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Dodgers de Los Ángeles.
- Juan Soto, Mets de Nueva York.
- Corey Seager, Texas Rangers.
- Vladimir Guerrero Jr., Toronto Blue Jays.
- Adley Rutschman, Medias Rojas de Boston.
- Kyle Schwarber, Filis de Filadelfia.
- Paul Skenes, Piratas de Pittsburgh.
- Cal Raleigh, Marineros de Seattle.
- Elly De La Cruz, Rojos de Cincinnati.
- Jackson Merrill, Padres de San Diego.
- Nolan Arenado, Arizona Diamondbacks.
- Munetaka Murakami, Chicago White Sox.
Shohei Ohtani encabeza por cuarto año consecutivo
El japonés Shohei Ohtani, de los Dodgers de Los Ángeles, volvió a ser el jugador con la camiseta más vendida de las Grandes Ligas, una posición que ocupa por cuarto año consecutivo.
Ohtani se convirtió así en el primer jugador en encadenar cuatro temporadas como líder en ventas de camisetas desde que MLB comenzó a registrar este dato en 2010, reseñó la agencia de noticias EFE este viernes 25 de septiembre.
Desde 2023, los aficionados han comprado la camiseta Nike de Ohtani más que cualquier otra en Estados Unidos, Japón y el resto del mundo, consolidando al jugador japonés como la figura con mayor demanda comercial entre los peloteros de las Grandes Ligas.
El listado, elaborado a partir de las ventas de camisetas Nike realizadas a través de Fanatics, incluido MLBShop.com, desde el Día Inaugural de la temporada 2026, sitúa al capitán de los Yankees de Nueva York, Aaron Judge, en el segundo puesto y al jardinero de los Cachorros de Chicago Pete Crow-Armstrong en el tercero.

item.title: [CBS Sports] Vladimir Guerrero Jr. apologizes for controversial comments about his $500 million contract
item.dc:creator: Dayn Perry
item.description: Toronto Blue Jays first baseman Vladimir Guerrero Jr. has apologized days after saying his $500 million contract extension rather than a reflection of his value moving forward. Guerrero Jr. on Friday, ahead of his team's season-ending home series against the Cincinnati Reds, issued the following statement, via MLB.com: "I want to tell everyone that I'm going to continue to keep working hard to make my contract a great one. … "I feel that the comments I made the other day is not what I really wan
item.content:encoded:
Toronto Blue Jays first baseman Vladimir Guerrero Jr. has apologized days after saying his $500 million contract extension rather than a reflection of his value moving forward.
Guerrero Jr. on Friday, ahead of his team's season-ending home series against the Cincinnati Reds, issued the following statement, via MLB.com:
"I want to tell everyone that I'm going to continue to keep working hard to make my contract a great one.
…
"I feel that the comments I made the other day is not what I really wanted to say. Everyone deserves an apology from me."
Guerrero Jr. said he regretted his comments and felt like he owed an apology to the fans and his teammates.
Vladdy starts his availability with a statement, through interpreter:
“The reason I'm here because I regret my comments the other day … I feel from my heart, my fans, my teammates, they needed an apology from me, and that's why I'm here for.”#BlueJays
Additionally, Guerrero Jr. said he decided to apologize after speaking with his father, Hall of Famer Vladimir Guerrero Sr.
The controversy stemmed from what the 27-year-old first baseman recently told Telemicro News, as translated by Héctor Gómez:
"The contract I got was based on what I did, not necessarily for what I'm going to do. I understand why the fans believe it's the other way around. Sometimes I think that way too, like 'oh they give me this money and I'm not doing enough', but you know I try my best and I'm working hard.
"The fans I know how they are, when you are doing great they are 100% behind you but when you are not at your best not everybody is behind you, almost nobody supports you. Those are my real fans, the ones that are supporting me all the time."
Guerrero Jr.'s original comments were ill-timed, as the reigning American League champion Blue Jays have been eliminated from playoff contention, and Guerrero Jr. himself has endured a highly disappointing season:
The above comes to an OPS+ of just 92, or a park-adjusted OPS that's 8% worse than the league average. Coming into 2026, he had a career OPS+ of 136. This season, Guerrero Jr. has hit just nine home runs and only one at home. He's slugged just .360, and his WAR has dropped from 4.6 a season ago to 1.3 in 2026. This decline in production has come in the first year of that $500 million extension, which will run through the 2039 season.
The only way Guerrero Jr. can truly put those struggles behind him is with a strong 2027, and his words on Friday suggest he's dedicated to making that happen.
The last-place Blue Jays enter the final weekend of the regular season with a record of 77-82, which means they've ensured a losing season for the second time in the last three years.

item.content:encoded:
The Toronto Blue Jays have endured a highly disappointing season after winning the American League last year.
The Blue Jays have now officially been eliminated from MLB postseason contention after being swept by the Baltimore Orioles earlier this week. The team struggled to find consistent production throughout the season, and now sits in last place in the AL East at 77-82.
One of the biggest disappointments during an overall frustrating season has been first baseman Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
The six-time All-Star signed a 14-year, $500 million extension with Toronto in April of 2025 and followed it with an excellent season and a trip to the World Series. However, in the 2026 season, he has seen a steep drop-off in production.
A season to forget
Sep 18, 2026; Arlington, Texas, USA; Toronto Blue Jays first baseman Vladimir Guerrero Jr. (27) walks to the dugout after the end of the fifth inning against the Texas Rangers at Globe Life Field. Mandatory Credit: Raymond Carlin III-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)
Guerrero is slashing .263/.335/.360 with just nine home runs and 56 RBIs in 142 games. His .695 OPS is the lowest mark of his career. With Toronto's season effectively over, Guerrero's recent comments surrounding his contract were met with a flurry of scrutiny.
In a conversation with Veronica Batista, Guerrero said in Spanish, "The money they gave me wasn't for what I'm going to do. It was for what I already did. They didn't pay me because I'm going to hit 40 every year. They paid me for what I already accomplished."
Given his struggles this season, fans criticized the comments. Guerrero later stood by his remarks, making it clear he is not looking to avoid responsibility.
Guerrero has since received support from Hall of Fame pitcher Pedro Martínez, who is also Guerrero's godfather. Martínez defended Guerrero, stating he was misunderstood and was not intending to excuse his current performance.
Martínez pushes back
Phillip Feliz spoke with Martínez, who said, "He was misinterpreted. What he meant is that contract came from what he's already done, and what he can still do. That's a young man talking. He just didn't explain himself the right way."
Pedro Martínez, Vladdy's godfather, on the contract comments:
"He was misinterpreted. What he meant is that contract came from what he's already done, and what he can still do. That's a young man talking. He just didn't explain himself the right way." pic.twitter.com/W0wXvrGh5y
— Master Flip | Phillip Feliz 🇩🇴 (@Masterflip_) September 25, 2026
Guerrero's comments may have sounded poorly timed given his and the team's struggles this season. However, Martínez wants critics to know that the contract rewarded what Guerrero had already established while also reflecting the belief that he can still produce at a high level moving forward.
For Guerrero, a rebound at the plate next season will be the clearest way to move past this controversy. With 13 seasons left on his deal, he has plenty of time to show Blue Jays fans that he can live up to the expectations of his extension.

item.title: [sportingnews.com] Why Mariners' Cal Raleigh is AL's 'LVP' and not Vladimir Guerrero Jr. | Sporting News
item.dc:creator: Matt Sullivan

item.content:encoded:
The Seattle Mariners have had a rough 2026 season. After coming one win shy of the World Series a year ago, they've failed to make the postseason despite the AL West leader having a record under .500 with three games to go.
This Mariners season is one of the worst in recent years due to the expectations coming into the season. A lot of people are to blame, but one of the main reasons why things fell apart is thanks to Cal Raleigh.
Jayson Stark of The Athletic named Raleigh the American League's "LVP" or "Least Valuable Player." Instead of Vladimir Guerrero Jr. earning this label for his poor 2026 season, Raleigh is the LVP of the season for a few key reasons.
Why Cal Raleigh earned LVP award over Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
"The Mariners' catcher has gone from MVP runner-up, 60-homer machine and heartbeat of a team that was eight outs from the World Series to... eh, hoo boy," Stark writes. "The Big Dumper has been worth 1.1 WAR all season, according to Baseball Reference..."
Raleigh's drop-off this season isn't limited to just some struggles to accumulate bWAR. There is so much else that's gone wrong for the Mariners catcher.
"But would that alone have been enough to push Raleigh 'ahead' of Vladdy in this LVP derby? It would not," Stark writes. "To pull that off would have taken one of the steepest drop-offs, from one season to the next, in baseball history. Unfortunately for Raleigh, that's what he's enduring."
Raleigh has gone from 60 homers to 23 with three games to go. That's the biggest drop-off of all-time for a 60-homer hitter, according to Stark.
Regarding his 1.1 bWAR, Stark shared, "And if you're wondering how many top-two MVP finishers have ever gone from at least 7.0 that year to under 2. 0the next, that would be none -- until now."
Raleigh's drop-off in homers and bWAR is something baseball has never seen before. But it's so much more than just those two poor statistics.
He posted a slash line of .247/.359/.589 last season. In 2026, his average dropped 68 points, his on-base percentage 63 points, and his slugging percentage an astounding 220 points with three games to go.
Those numbers will look different by the end of the season, but those are some truly terrible drop-offs, even if he were to get hot in these final three games of 2026.
Going from a 169 OPS+ to a 92 OPS+, and a .948 OPS to a .663 OPS, is an all-time fall-off for any player in MLB history.
All of that is exceptionally terrible production, but considering Guerrero has just nine homers this season with a .695 OPS and a 92 OPS+, he's not the "LVP" this season due to the sheer drop-off from Raleigh in 2025 to 2026.
It's not just the drop-off for Raleigh that's playing a role here either. The Blue Jays had a rough 2026 season, but they at least played better than Seattle did this year.
Raleigh is the "LVP" of the American League in 2026 thanks to the record-breaking drop-off he's had from 2025 to 2026.
While he might not be the worst player in the AL, his production in 2026 is far below what was expected of him this season and is more than deserving of the "Least Valuable Player" label this year.

item.title: [bluejaysnation.com] Vladimir Guerrero Jr.’s not wrong, but he’s also not right
item.dc:creator: Ian Hunter
item.description: Vladimir Guerrero Jr.’s not wrong, but he’s also not right Photo credit: Cary Edmondson-Imagn Images The Toronto Blue Jays’ offseason hasn’t even begun, but the club is already the talk of baseball thanks to the face of their franchise, Vladimir Guerrero Jr. He may have put his foot in his mouth when his comments made the rounds earlier this week after an interview with podcaster Veronica Batista. Guerrero seemed to express remorse about his disappointing season, but his remarks weren’t perceive
item.content:encoded:
Vladimir Guerrero Jr.’s not wrong, but he’s also not right
Photo credit: Cary Edmondson-Imagn Images
The Toronto Blue Jays’ offseason hasn’t even begun, but the club is already the talk of baseball thanks to the face of their franchise, Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
He may have put his foot in his mouth when his comments made the rounds earlier this week after an interview with podcaster Veronica Batista. Guerrero seemed to express remorse about his disappointing season, but his remarks weren’t perceived that way by some fans.
First of all, the timing of this interview could not have been worse. The video came out the day the Blue Jays were eliminated from postseason contention. It’s almost as if it were planned that way for maximum exposure and general outrage.
Had this interview taken place earlier this season, or during the offseason, there would be a different tenor about it. But with a lot of vitriol among the Blue Jays fan base, these comments have not sat well among Jays devotees.
There are some areas where he’s right and some areas where he’s wrong. The comment that drew the most ire was Guerrero saying, “They didn’t pay me because I’m going to hit 40 every year. They paid me for what I already accomplished.”
Is this Vladdy saying the quiet part out loud, or is there credence to what he said?
Professional baseball players are criminally underpaid at the beginning of their careers. To earn the league minimum through the first three years of their Major League journey, followed by three years of arbitration (four if you’re lucky to reach Super Two status), is a big reason many teams can afford to keep their productive players.
The value that Guerrero provided at the beginning of his career far exceeded what he was paid before he signed his monster contract. According to FanGraphs’ Value metric, Vladdy provided $164 million in value through his first seven seasons in the big leagues while earning $72.5 million.
Anyone aside from MLB owners would agree the salary arbitration model is broken, so it’s easy to see why Guerrero feels like his $500 million contract is a delayed payment for his early-career production. Surely, there are many MLB players who are silently yelling “PREACH” after hearing what Guerrero said.
In that moment, Vlad was acting as an advocate for his fellow players. Given that the players and owners are hurtling toward a lockout on December 2, his stance was understandable. He is one of the faces of Major League Baseball, so as Vlad goes, so too does the rest of the league.
But that’s not how modern-day contracts work. Nine-figure deals paying for past production may be a Pollyanna perspective held by some professional athletes, but those contracts bank on future production more than the past. As much as MLB executives might spin it to the players as a thank you for services tendered, it’s not totally accurate.
Guerrero should be given some grace, as not everything he said in the video (and the follow-up comments) was flame-worthy. In a way, he admitted the pressure of the $500 million contract is weighing on him, which is to be expected for any 27-year-old handed the keys to the Blue Jays for the next 13 years.
Although Guerrero surely meant no harm during that interview, he had to have known his comments would be unnerving to folks in Toronto. The optics are bad, and this is a PR blunder. At the very least, his handlers should’ve had a better grasp on the temperature of the Blue Jays fan base and asked to delay the release of the interview, rather than have it drop at the worst possible moment.
After the disappointing season Vlad had, some fans wanted their pound of flesh, and anything less than a full admission of ineptitude wouldn’t suffice. When a player carries a team like Guerrero did in the postseason last year and then virtually disappears the following season, people want answers.
Vlad didn’t have an answer that made anyone feel better about how 2026 went down, which may be the underlying reason for all this venom in the first place. Guerrero can’t just “aw shucks” a single-digit home run total and sub-.700 OPS season away, but for baseball players, compartmentalizing failure is what makes them successful.
Had Vladdy missed significant time this season due to injuries, there would be a little more tolerance for his underperformance. The fact that he played 140+ games this year, claiming to not be injured, almost makes it worse because his regression can’t be blamed on an injury.
I don’t believe the Blue Jays have buyer’s remorse already, but this is the risk you run plunking a half-billion dollars into one player. If they carry the team on their back, they’re the GOAT. If they fail, they’re the goat.
It’s an apples-to-oranges situation, but the Boston Red Sox ran Rafael Devers out of town after giving him the keys to Beantown. A few years after inking a 10-year, $331 million extension, the fracture between Devers and the Red Sox front office grew so wide that he was traded to the San Francisco Giants.
I’m not saying the same fate befalls Toronto’s golden child, but we’re already starting to witness the side effects of tying up so much money in one player. The fan base hasn’t turned on Guerrero, but this could start to get ugly if he fails to turn things around in 2027.
2026 will not only be remembered as a golden opportunity missed by the Blue Jays but also by Vladdy himself. Guerrero wasn’t wrong with many of the things he said, but he also wasn’t right. The timing was atrocious, but hey, isn’t that typical of Toronto sports?
Sponsored by bet365

item.title: [Sportsnet.ca] 'It's emotional to think about': George Springer faces end of Blue Jays deal
